name: Wraith-Ossuary
geological_features: Dry cave systems with mineral formations
specific_features: Surface deposits that resemble skeletal remains at macro scale
Calcium formations in caves shaped by ancient water flow into arch and column patterns
description: Wraith-Ossuary is a barren world whose surface is covered in thick deposits of calcium carbonate that give the landscape the bleached-white appearance of sun-dried bone. The deposits are biological in origin, the accumulated remains of a marine ecosystem that died when the planet lost its ocean approximately five hundred million years ago. Erosion has sculpted the calcium layers into formations that bear an unsettling resemblance to skeletal structures, ridges that look like ribs, mounds that suggest skulls, pillars that could be femurs standing upright in white soil.

The thin atmosphere supports hazy twilights and pale dawns, the calcium surface reflecting so much light that the planet appears to glow even under faint stellar illumination. Karst sinkholes dot the surface where ancient rainwater dissolved the calcium deposits before the atmosphere thinned beyond the point of precipitation, their circular mouths opening into cave systems that extend for kilometers beneath the surface. The silence is near-total, the thin air carrying only the faintest whisper of wind across the bone-white plains.

The cave systems preserve formations created during the planet's wet epoch, calcium carbonate stalactites and flowstone deposits shaped by water that has not flowed for half a billion years. The formations are pristine, no biological activity or atmospheric chemistry has degraded them since the last drops evaporated. Some chambers contain what appear to be fossilized remains of the marine organisms whose bodies became the surface deposits, creatures with calcium shells of elaborate architecture that lived in shallow seas under a thicker, warmer atmosphere.

Wraith-Ossuary's calcium and phosphorus deposits are commercially valuable as raw materials for agricultural fertilizer and construction applications. The fossilized marine remains are of scientific interest but too fragile for casual extraction, the calcium structures crumbling to powder under rough handling. A small mining operation processes surface deposits in the equatorial band, where temperatures are most moderate, while a research team catalogs the cave formations and fossils in an ongoing survey that has so far mapped less than five percent of the subterranean network.
